doc.title: Don Wolff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Decline of dancing after World War II
summary: Wolff says dancing faded after the war as big bands declined, and Rowe cites a musician on swing versus even eighth notes.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Marvelous. What effect did the dancing that was so connected with jazz, and at the end of World War II I guess, do you have a take on what kind of happened at that point?

Well a number of things happened. Number one America got out of the dance phase quote unquote. The art of dance was very, very important both to jazz and vice versa. Not only in Hollywood, but in the early days of jazz, jazz was associated with dancing. Even Glenn Miller quote unquote jazz. The people when they really got to enjoying Glenn Miller and Benny Goodman, jitterbugged. So it wasn’t just music to crowd around the bandstand and listen to, it was music to dance to and the same thing was true with Ellington and Basie. But I think after the war, people stopped dancing as much as they did before. For some reason or another, the craze, the dance craze sort of disappeared from the face of America. Whether it was because it was a time of less pleasure and more work and more need to generate income and the cost of entertainment was a questionable item or not, an economic reason or not, I’m not sure. But when you look back at the period you see that the jitterbug phase and the dancing to jazz faded out right shortly after the war, World War II.

I sometimes wonder if there wasn’t enough stress after World War II. I mean the dancing could have been a release because there were tough times and there was a war and all that, and when that went away, maybe people didn’t feel that need to—

Well you know the big bands disappeared — certainly were reduced in number and popularity and economically they didn’t survive, only a few of the big bands survived. So as the big band sound disappeared, so did the dancing that went with the big bands. Now we got all kinds of other dancing that came in but it’s not associated with jazz. And I remember when the twist came in and the limbo came in, and although that wasn’t jazz, you know, it wasn’t far off from jazz and of course jazz has gone off into Brazilian and South American trends. And there is some dancing that goes on with that kind of music.

One of the musicians we talked to seemed to sum up the whole thing he said well music switched from swing eighth notes to even eighth notes. And that just about said it all. Because even eighth notes became rock & roll.
From a musician’s point of view that was a good answer.
